steps.step_short_description: Confirm the petitioner and the child qualify for IR-2
steps.step_description: Only U.S. citizens may petition for an immediate relative child (IR-2). Lawful permanent residents cannot petition under the IR-2 immediate relative category, they must use a different family preference category (F-2A). The petitioner must be a U.S. citizen. IR-2 is the immediate relative immigrant visa category for an unmarried child under 21 of a U.S. citizen. As an immediate relative, there is no visa number waiting line, the visa is available immediately upon I-130 approval and NVC completion. Note on CR-2: The CR-2 category refers to a child who immigrates as a derivative of a conditional resident (CR-1) parent. If you are petitioning your child directly as a U.S. citizen, the applicable category is IR-2, not CR-2.

steps.step_short_description: Relationship and civil documents for an IR-2 child petition
steps.step_description: Biological child: For a biological child, the petitioner must be the legal (natural) parent. A child born in wedlock requires proof of the parent-child blood relationship and that the parents were married at or before the child's birth. Stepchild: A stepchild qualifies as a 'child' for immigration purposes if the marriage creating the step-relationship occurred before the child's 18th birthday. The petitioner (the stepparent) must be the U.S. citizen who is married to the child's biological parent. See INA Sec. 101(b)(1)(B). Important: The qualifying marriage must have taken place BEFORE the child turned 18. If the marriage occurred after the child's 18th birthday, the stepchild does not qualify as an IR-2 under this rule. Adopted child: An adopted child qualifies if the adoption was legally completed before the child turned 16 (or before age 18 if the child is an orphan or adopted with a sibling), and the child has been in the legal custody of and resided with the adopting parent(s) for at least 2 years. See INA Sec. 101(b)(1)(E). Adoption cases can be complex. Requirements vary based on when the adoption was finalized, which country the child is from (Hague Convention vs. non-Hague), and whether the '2-year custody and residence' requirement is met. Consulting an immigration attorney is strongly recommended for adoption-based petitions. Guardianship (for example a guardianship order from a Pakistani court) is not automatically treated as an adoption for IR-2. If the child is in your care under guardianship, speak with a qualified U.S. immigration attorney before filing. Before filing Form I-130, collect all civil documents needed to prove the qualifying relationship and the petitioner's citizenship. Documents not in English must be accompanied by a certified English translation.

guide_steps.text: After selecting I-130, the page shows the current filing fees for Form I-130. Review the fee for Paper Filing before preparing your payment. Have the exact amount ready before assembling the final mailing packet.
guide_steps.note: You are filing by paper, so the applicable fee is the Paper Filing Fee. Prepare payment for this exact amount before packet assembly.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Choose your paper-filing payment method
guide_steps.text:
USCIS no longer accepts personal/business checks, money orders, or cashier's checks. You must use one of the approved payment or fee exemption options:
  • Option A: Pay by credit, debit, or prepaid card using Form G-1450 (Authorization for Credit Card Transactions).
  • Option B: Pay from a U.S. bank account (ACH) using Form G-1650.
  • Option C: If eligible for an exemption from the higher paper filing fee, submit Form G-1651 (Exemption for Paper Fee Payment).
USCIS Form G-1651 Exemption Requirements
To request an exemption, you must certify that electronic payment and collection methods are not possible and you meet 1 or more of the following requirements:
  • You do not have access to banking services or electronic payment systems;
  • Electronic disbursement would cause you undue hardship (infrastructure barriers in remote/foreign areas or personal limitations), as discussed in 31 C.F.R. Part 208 (GovInfo Official Citation ↗);
  • Non-electronic transactions are necessary or desirable for national security or law enforcement reasons; or
  • There are other circumstances as determined by the secretary of the treasury, as reflected in regulations or other guidance.
Hardship categories under 31 C.F.R. Sec. 208.4: Infrastructure barriers (foreign/remote regions lacking U.S. digital banking) and personal barriers (financial, physical, or technical inability to manage online banking).
guide_steps.note: Download and print Form G-1450, Form G-1650, or Form G-1651 from uscis.gov and fill it out completely before placing it in the packet.

guide_steps.label: Payment guide · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Place payment at the front of the packet
guide_steps.text: Once the payment item is ready, whether it is a completed Form G-1450 (card), Form G-1650 (ACH), or Form G-1651 (Fee Exemption), place it at the very front of the mailing packet. The payment or fee exemption form should be the first thing USCIS sees when they open the envelope.

guide_steps.text: Organize the completed paper filing into one final mailing packet before shipment. steps.step_description: During USCIS review, USCIS may issue a notice requesting additional evidence or information before making a decision. Identify the notice type so Rahvana can guide your specific response.

tool_data.title: USCIS Notice Received
tool_data.subtitle: USCIS may ask for additional evidence or information before deciding your petition. Identify the notice type below so Rahvana can guide your response.

alert.heading: Do not ignore this notice
alert.body: Missing the response deadline can result in your petition being denied, including denial based on abandonment. USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period.

intro_card.heading: Receiving a USCIS notice is not the end of the road
intro_card.body: Most notices give you an opportunity to respond before a final decision is made. The key is to read the notice carefully, respond to exactly what USCIS asked for, and submit a complete response before the deadline.

notice_types.label: I-797, Approval Notice
notice_types.description: USCIS has approved your I-130 petition and issued an I-797 approval notice. Save the original notice and prepare for the NVC stage.

notice_types.label: RFE, Request for Evidence
notice_types.description: USCIS needs additional evidence or information before it can decide your petition. This is the most common notice. Receiving an RFE does not mean your petition has been denied.

notice_types.label: RFI, Request for Additional Information
notice_types.description: USCIS is asking for clarifying information. Similar in nature to an RFE but typically more limited in scope.

notice_types.label: RFO, Request for Original Document
notice_types.description: USCIS is requesting an original document. You may have submitted a copy where an original is required.

notice_types.label: NOID, Notice of Intent to Deny
notice_types.description: USCIS is considering denying your petition and is giving you a chance to respond. This is more serious than an RFE. Consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

notice_types.label: Denial, I-130 Petition Denied
notice_types.description: USCIS has issued a denial of your I-130 petition. Review the denial notice carefully, it explains the reasons and your available options such as appeal or motion.

notice_types.label: Other USCIS notice or request
notice_types.description: USCIS may send other types of requests such as biometrics appointments or interview notices. Follow the specific instructions on your notice.

where_to_find.title: Where to find your notice

items.detail: Log in to my.uscis.gov and check your case notices and messages. USCIS recommends checking your online account first.
Notices may also be sent by mail to the petitioner's address on file. Keep your address updated with USCIS.

where_to_find.note: If your USCIS online account shows an RFE, an online response portal may be available. Do not mail a duplicate response if you submit online.

deadline_warning.heading: Check the deadline on your actual notice
deadline_warning.body: Do not assume you have a specific number of days. The deadline is printed on your RFE or NOID notice. USCIS states that the maximum response period is generally 12 weeks, but the notice controls the actual deadline for your case.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Evidence · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS may issue a Request for Evidence (RFE) or Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) if additional information or documents are needed. Respond fully before the stated deadline.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Additional Information · Prepare & submit response
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for Additional Information (RFI) on your I-130 petition. An RFI typically requests clarifying information and is generally narrower in scope than an RFE.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFI
guide_data.subtitle: A Request for Additional Information (RFI) means USCIS needs specific clarifying information before proceeding. Read the notice carefully and respond directly to what is asked.

alert.heading: An RFI does not mean your petition was denied
alert.body: USCIS is requesting clarifying information to continue processing your petition. Respond to exactly what is asked, before the deadline printed on the notice.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the RFI notice
guide_steps.text: Check your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or your physical mail for the RFI notice. Read the notice carefully to understand exactly what information USCIS is requesting.
guide_steps.note: An RFI is typically narrower in scope than an RFE. USCIS is asking for specific clarifying information, not a broad set of evidence.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFI notice. Note it immediately and plan your response with enough time to review everything before submitting.
guide_steps.note: USCIS generally does not grant extensions beyond the permitted response period. Missing the deadline can result in a denial.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Prepare a clear, direct response
guide_steps.text: Respond directly to the information USCIS requested. Provide only what is asked, clear, focused, and accurate. Include a brief cover letter that identifies what was requested and how your response addresses it.
guide_steps.note: Clarity is key. A focused response that directly answers the question is more effective than a large unorganized package.

guide_steps.label: RFI Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit one complete response
guide_steps.text: Assemble your complete response into a single submission. Do not submit in pieces. Use the submission method specified in your RFI notice, online portal if available in your USCIS account, or mail if instructed.
guide_steps.note: If submitting online, do not also mail a duplicate response. Keep a copy of everything you submit.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you are uncertain about your RFI response, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Request for Original Document · Locate & submit original
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Request for an Original (RFO) document. USCIS is requesting that you submit the original version of a document you may have previously submitted as a copy.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS RFO
guide_data.subtitle: USCIS is requesting an original document. Identify the specific document requested, locate the original, and submit it following the instructions on your notice.

alert.heading: USCIS is asking for an original, not a copy
alert.body: Carefully read your RFO notice to identify exactly which document is required in original form. Submitting another copy will not satisfy the request.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Identify the specific document requested
guide_steps.text: Read your RFO notice carefully. USCIS will identify the specific document it is requesting in original form. Common examples include original birth certificates, original marriage certificates/Nikah Namas, or other original civil documents.
guide_steps.note: If you are unsure whether your document is truly the original versus a certified copy, contact the issuing authority to clarify.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline
guide_steps.text: The deadline is printed on your RFO notice. Mark it immediately. Plan enough time to locate the document, make a copy for your records, and prepare your submission.
guide_steps.note: Do not wait until close to the deadline. Locating original documents, especially civil documents from Pakistan, may take time.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Make a copy before submitting the original
guide_steps.text: Before sending any original document to USCIS, make a clear copy for your own records. USCIS receives many documents and originals are not always returned promptly, or may take significant time to be returned.
guide_steps.note: Keep your copy in a safe place. If the original is irreplaceable, consider consulting an immigration attorney about the best approach.

guide_steps.label: RFO Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Submit using a secure, trackable method
guide_steps.text: Send the original document using a secure and trackable shipping method. Include a cover letter identifying the case receipt number, the RFO reference, and what document is enclosed. Follow the submission instructions in your RFO notice.
guide_steps.note: Keep the tracking number and delivery confirmation. Once the carrier shows delivered, save that proof.

guide_data.disclaimer: Rahvana provides structured guidance only. This is not legal advice. If you have concerns about submitting irreplaceable original documents, consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney.

steps.step_short_description: Notice of Intent to Deny · Respond carefully before deadline
steps.step_description: USCIS has issued a Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) on your I-130 petition. A NOID is more serious than an RFE, USCIS is indicating it is considering denying your petition based on the current record and is giving you one opportunity to respond.

guide_data.title: Respond to USCIS NOID
guide_data.subtitle: A Notice of Intent to Deny (NOID) means USCIS is considering denying your petition. This is your opportunity to respond with evidence and legal arguments before a final decision is made.

alert.heading: A NOID is more serious than an RFE
alert.body: USCIS is not simply asking for more evidence. It is indicating that based on the current record, it intends to deny your petition, and is giving you one opportunity to respond. Carefully review the reasons USCIS has stated. Because the response may require legal analysis, strongly consider getting help from a qualified immigration attorney.

noid_vs_rfe.title: NOID vs. RFE, the key difference

rfe.label: RFE
rfe.description: We need more evidence before we can make a decision.

noid.label: NOID
noid.description: Based on what we currently have, we are considering denying your petition. Here is why. You have one opportunity to respond.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Obtain and read the NOID notice immediately
guide_steps.text: Obtain the NOID notice from your USCIS online account at my.uscis.gov or from physical mail. Read the entire notice carefully. USCIS is required to identify the intended reasons for denial, explain deficiencies, and identify potentially missing evidence.
guide_steps.note: Understanding exactly what USCIS says is wrong is the foundation of your response. Do not skip or skim any part of the notice.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Check the response deadline immediately
guide_steps.text: The response deadline is printed on your NOID notice. Note it immediately and treat it as your hard deadline. Extensions are generally not granted.
guide_steps.note: Given the seriousness of a NOID, you should begin working on your response immediately, do not wait until close to the deadline.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Because a NOID response may require legal analysis and argumentation, not just evidence submission, strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney before preparing your response. An attorney can assess the specific deficiencies USCIS identified and advise on the best response strategy.
guide_steps.note: This is Rahvana's strongest recommendation for NOID situations. The consequences of a denial are significant, the response deserves careful legal attention.

guide_steps.label: NOID Response · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Address each stated reason for the proposed denial
guide_steps.text: Your response must directly address each reason USCIS stated in the NOID. For each issue identified, explain why that reason does not support denial and provide evidence that counters or clarifies the issue.

guide_data.title: I-130 Denied, Review Your Options
guide_data.subtitle: An I-130 denial is a serious outcome, but it may not be the end of the road. Review the denial notice carefully and understand what options may be available.

alert.heading: Carefully review the denial notice
alert.body: The denial notice explains USCIS's specific reasons for the denial and states what appeal or motion options are available in your case. The correct next step depends entirely on the specific reasons for the denial and the facts of your case. Do not file an appeal or motion without understanding the denial first.

denial_options.title: Possible options after an I-130 denial
denial_options.subtitle: Which option is appropriate depends on the specific reasons for the denial and the circumstances of your case. The denial notice itself explains what options are available.

options.label: Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA)
options.description: Certain I-130 decisions can be appealed to the Board of Immigration Appeals using Form EOIR-29 (Notice of Appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals from a Decision of a DHS Officer). USCIS confirms that I-130 appeals are among the appeals filed using Form EOIR-29.
options.important: Appeals have strict deadlines. Check your denial notice for the deadline and the specific appeal procedure that applies to your case.

options.label: Motion to Reopen
options.description: A motion to reopen asks USCIS to reopen the case based on new facts or evidence that was not available at the time of the decision.
options.important: A motion to reopen is appropriate when there is new factual evidence that was not part of the original record. Review the denial carefully before pursuing this option.

options.label: Motion to Reconsider
options.description: A motion to reconsider asks USCIS to reconsider its decision based on an error of law or incorrect application of policy to the existing facts.
options.important: A motion to reconsider is appropriate when you believe USCIS made a legal error in the denial, not when you simply have new evidence.

options.label: File a new petition
options.description: Depending on the denial reason, it may sometimes be appropriate to file a new I-130 petition with corrected information or additional evidence. This should be carefully evaluated based on the specific denial reason.
options.important: Filing a new petition when an appeal or motion is more appropriate may not be the best strategy. Consult an immigration attorney.

attorney_recommendation.heading: Strongly consider consulting a qualified immigration attorney
attorney_recommendation.body: Determining the right strategy after an I-130 denial, appeal vs. motion vs. new petition, requires careful analysis of the denial reasons, the evidence record, and the applicable law. The wrong choice can waste time, resources, or foreclose other options. An experienced immigration attorney can help you evaluate the best path forward.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 1
guide_steps.title: Read the denial notice completely
guide_steps.text: The denial notice contains the specific reasons USCIS denied the petition and explains what appeal or motion rights are available. Read it completely before deciding on any next step.
guide_steps.note: The denial notice is the most important document at this stage. Every option you consider must be evaluated against the specific reasons stated in the notice.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 2
guide_steps.title: Note any deadlines for appeal or motion
guide_steps.text: If the denial notice indicates appeal or motion rights, it will also state the deadlines for filing. These deadlines are strict, missing them can eliminate certain options.
guide_steps.note: Do not delay in reviewing the notice and understanding the available deadlines. Begin consulting an attorney as soon as possible if you are considering an appeal or motion.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 3
guide_steps.title: Consult a qualified immigration attorney
guide_steps.text: Given the complexity of determining the right post-denial strategy, consulting a qualified immigration attorney is strongly recommended. An attorney can review the denial notice, assess the options, and advise on the best course of action specific to your case.
guide_steps.note: Do not treat this as optional. The stakes of an I-130 denial are high, and the correct path forward requires professional evaluation.

guide_steps.label: After Denial · Step 4
guide_steps.title: Evaluate and act on the appropriate option
guide_steps.text: Based on the denial reasons and legal advice, determine whether an appeal (Form EOIR-29 to the BIA), a motion to reopen, a motion to reconsider, or another strategy is appropriate. Act within the applicable deadlines.
guide_steps.note: Rahvana can guide you through general information about each option, but the final decision on which path to take should be made with qualified legal assistance.

visual.title: Why this is required

guideSteps.label: Step 2 of 5
guideSteps.heading: Where to get vaccinated
guideSteps.instruction: Polio vaccinations for visa purposes must be obtained from an approved government vaccination post or official WHO-designated site. Do not use a private clinic unless it is specifically on the approved list.
guideSteps.note: Do not go to a general doctor or hospital for this, you must use a government-approved site for the certificate to be accepted.

Vaccine type, oral polio vaccine (OPV)

doc_relationship.title: Relationship Evidence
doc_relationship.sub: Proof the marriage is genuine and entered in good faith

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.htmlContent: USCIS adjudicators will assess whether the marriage is bona fide, entered in good faith for a genuine life together, not primarily to obtain immigration benefits. Evidence across multiple categories significantly strengthens the case.

sections.title: Strong evidence categories
sections.htmlContent:
Gather evidence across as many of these categories as possible:

  • Communication history, WhatsApp/call logs, screenshots of messages over time, email correspondence showing an ongoing relationship
  • Photos together, wedding photos, casual photos, photos across different dates and locations, family gatherings
  • Travel history, plane tickets, boarding passes, hotel bookings showing in-person visits
  • Shared finances, joint bank account statements, shared bills, financial transfers between spouses
  • Shared residence, lease agreements, utility bills, or mail showing a shared address
  • Family evidence, children together, family photos that show integration into each other's families
  • Affidavits, signed statements from family members or friends who personally know the couple and can attest to the relationship

sections.title: For the I-130 stage specifically
sections.htmlContent:
At the USCIS I-130 filing stage, the petitioner submits the I-130 along with supporting evidence. A strong bona fide marriage package typically includes:

  • At least 3-5 photos showing the couple together across different occasions
  • Evidence of ongoing communication (call logs or chat screenshots with metadata)
  • Evidence of at least one in-person visit (travel documentation)
  • Affidavits if direct joint evidence is limited

There is no single "required" evidence list from USCIS, the goal is to present a convincing overall picture of a genuine relationship. More varied evidence across categories is better than one large category alone.

sections.title: What to avoid
sections.htmlContent:
• Do not submit hundreds of pages of chat history, curate and organize
  • Avoid submitting only one type of evidence (e.g. photos only)
  • Ensure affidavits are signed, dated, and specific about how the writer knows the couple
  • Do not use generic template affidavits, they are easily spotted and carry little weight

doc_prior_marriage.title: Prior Marriage Termination Proof
doc_prior_marriage.sub: Required if either spouse had a previous marriage

sections.title: When this applies
sections.htmlContent:
This document is required if either the petitioner or the beneficiary was previously married. USCIS must confirm that every prior marriage ended legally before the current marriage began.

If neither spouse has a prior marriage, this item does not apply to your case.

sections.title: Accepted termination documents
sections.htmlContent:
• Divorce decree or divorce certificate, final court order ending the prior marriage
  • Annulment order, court order declaring the marriage void
  • Death certificate, if the prior spouse is deceased

sections.title: Pakistan-specific, divorce
sections.htmlContent:
In Pakistan, divorce proceedings vary by religious law. For Muslims, the process typically involves:

  • Talaq, the husband's pronouncement, registered with the Union Council, followed by a mandatory 90-day reconciliation period (iddat); Union Council issues a divorce certificate after this period
  • Khula, wife-initiated dissolution through Family Court; court issues the final decree
  • Judicial divorce, through Family Court; court issues the final decree

Important: For talaq, the divorce is not legally effective in Pakistan until the 90-day reconciliation period expires and the Union Council issues the divorce certificate. Ensure you have the final certificate, not just the initial notice.

sections.title: Translation requirement
sections.htmlContent: All divorce decrees and termination documents in Urdu or other non-English languages must be accompanied by a full certified English translation.

doc_translations.title: Translations
doc_translations.sub: Certified English translations of non-English documents

sections.title: USCIS translation requirement
sections.htmlContent: USCIS requires that every document not in English be accompanied by a full certified English translation. This applies to all stages, I-130, NVC, and consular.

sections.title: What "certified translation" means
sections.htmlContent:
USCIS defines a certified translation as one accompanied by a signed statement from the translator certifying:

  • They are competent to translate from the source language to English
  • The translation is accurate and complete to the best of their ability

The translator does not need to be a licensed professional or a notary, but they must not be the applicant or petitioner themselves.

sections.title: Documents that need translation
sections.htmlContent:
• Nikah Nama, typically in Urdu; full translation required
  • NADRA MRC, bilingual, but full translation of the Urdu portions is recommended to avoid questions
  • Birth certificate, if issued in Urdu or regional language
  • Divorce decree, if in Urdu or Sindhi etc.
  • Any other civil documents submitted to USCIS or the NVC

sections.title: Practical tips
sections.htmlContent:
• Use a translation service that issues a formal certification letter on their letterhead, it is more persuasive than a plain self-attestation
  • Keep the translated document together with the original, submit them as a pair
  • Do not translate only part of a document, the entire document must be translated

doc_passport_photos.title: Passport Photos
doc_passport_photos.sub: Required at consular and visa application stages

sections.title: When these are needed
sections.htmlContent:
Passport photos are not required for the USCIS I-130 petition filing. They are required at later stages:

  • The DS-260 immigrant visa application (online form submitted to the NVC)
  • At the consular interview, the U.S. Embassy in Islamabad typically requires passport-size photos

Gather them closer to those stages rather than now.

sections.title: U.S. visa photo specifications
sections.htmlContent:
• 2 × 2 inches (51 × 51 mm)
  • White or off-white plain background
  • Taken within the last 6 months
  • Full front view, neutral expression, eyes open
  • No glasses (as of 2016 U.S. visa photo rules)
  • Head coverings only for religious reasons, and must not obscure the face

The DS-260 online application accepts a digital photo upload, check the U.S. State Department's photo upload tool and specifications at the time of filing.

doc_name_change.title: Name Change or Identity Discrepancy Evidence
doc_name_change.sub: Resolving spelling and profile mismatches across records

sections.title: Handling Name Mismatches
sections.htmlContent: Mismatches across your birth certificate, national ID, school records, or passport can trigger delays or Requests for Evidence in any country, so it's worth sorting these out before you file.

sections.title: Civil Registry Correction
sections.htmlContent: To correct a name or date of birth, visit your country's civil registry office with supporting documents like matriculation certificates, older passports, or court decrees. In Pakistan, this means a NADRA office, which will issue a revised CNIC/NICOP and FRC. Note that NADRA generally only corrects English-spelling mistakes through this process, a full name change requires the separate procedure below.

sections.title: Gazette Notification & Deed Poll
sections.htmlContent: For a full legal name change in Pakistan, you'll need a notarized affidavit, a published notice in local newspapers, and registration with the official Gazette of Pakistan. The published Gazette notice is what carries real legal weight, it's what banks, passport offices, and other institutions will actually ask to see.

sections.title: Sworn Affidavits
sections.htmlContent: If your records genuinely can't be corrected, a notarized affidavit from close relatives explaining the mismatch can serve as backup evidence in most jurisdictions.

marriage-cert-hh.title: Marriage Certificate, Household Member
marriage-cert-hh.intro: Establishes the spousal relationship between the household member and the petitioner.

sections.title: What this is
sections.body: The civil marriage certificate proving that the household member is legally married to the petitioner. For Pakistan cases, this is the Nikah Nama and/or NADRA MRC.

sections.title: Why it is needed
sections.body: When the petitioner's spouse is acting as a household member contributing income through Form I-864A, the marriage must be documented to support that household connection.

sections.title: Translation
sections.body: The Nikah Nama (in Urdu) requires a full certified English translation.

shared-residence.title: Proof of Shared Residence
shared-residence.intro: Demonstrates that the household member and the petitioner share the same household address.

sections.title: What this is
sections.body: Documents showing a shared residential address between the petitioner and the household member. This reinforces the household income contribution basis.

sections.title: Accepted examples
sections.body:
• Lease agreement naming both parties
  • Utility bills addressed to the same household
  • Bank statements or tax returns showing the same address
  • Official correspondence addressed to both at the same address

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.body: The household member concept in I-864A depends on a genuine shared household. Residence proof strengthens the basis for including their income.

id-doc-hh.title: Identity Document, Household Member
id-doc-hh.intro: Confirms the identity of the household member named in the I-864A.

sections.title: What to provide
sections.body: A government-issued identity document for the household member. For Pakistan cases, this is typically the CNIC (Computerized National Identity Card) or a passport biographic page.

sections.title: Consistency
sections.body: The name on the identity document must match exactly the name used in CEAC and on the I-864A form. Any discrepancy should be explained or corrected.

family-link.title: Supporting Family-Link Evidence
family-link.intro: Used when the household member's relationship is more distant or non-standard, to establish the household connection.

sections.title: When this applies
sections.body: For household members who are other relatives (aunt, uncle, cousin, non-relative household member), standard civil records like birth certificates may not directly show the link. Additional supporting evidence helps.

sections.title: What to include
sections.body:
• Family tree documentation or affidavit of relationship
  • Any relevant civil records showing the family connection
  • Shared address or financial co-dependence records

sections.title: Note
sections.body: For non-standard relationships, consulting an immigration attorney before relying on household member income is strongly recommended.
